SEOUL, South Korea (CNN)  -- South Korea will open its market to most U.S. beef, a senior government official said Thursday, according to state media. Thousands of people have taken to the streets of the South Korean capital in protest at the deal . South Korea banned imports of U.S. beef in 2003 amid concerns over a case of mad cow disease in the United States. The ban closed what was then the third-largest market for U.S. beef exporters. It resumed limited imports last year -- allowing boneless beef from cattle under 30 months of age -- but that re-opening was subject to interruptions and closed altogether in October 2007. A deal that South Korea and the United States struck last month bans the import of high-risk materials, like tonsils, brains, spinal cord marrow and a section of the small intestine, Agriculture Minister Chung Woon-chun said Thursday, according to South Korea's Yonhap news agency. These parts pose the greatest risk of transmitting mad cow disease to humans. The ban will be lifted within a few days, once the government's new import rules have been published. The pending resumption of U.S. beef imports hasn't been without political costs for President Lee Myung-bak. He apologized to the nation last week for failing to fully understand concerns about mad cow disease. In downtown Seoul, thousands of people have regularly staged protests, chanting "We don't want crazy cows," since the deal to revive beef imports was announced. And the main opposition party has taken up the fight. "We will be forced to make a critical decision if the government pushes through its plan to announce resumption of beef imports," said Sohn Hak-kyu, leader of the main opposition United Democratic Party, Yonhap reported. "If the government and the ruling party ignore this warning, we will come up with every possible measure to stop them." The opposition has already filed a suit to suspend implementation of new beef import terms, according to Yonhap. Lee's ruling Grand National Party (GNP) is working to soothe tensions, saying that American beef is safe to eat and that adequate safety precautions have been taken. "The government has tried its best to free the public from unnecessary concerns, and sufficient countermeasures have been prepared," said Lee Hahn-koo, the party's chief policymaker, Yonhap reported. When South Korea and the United States reached the deal in April to re-open the South Korean market, they removed the major obstacle to U.S. congressional approval of the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (FTA). Lee urged the National Assembly this month to ratify the agreement as soon as possible to provide fresh impetus to the sluggish Korean economy, saying it will create 300,000 jobs. But the opposition has promised to fight the FTA until the beef pact is nullified. In 2003, the United States exported $815 million pounds of beef and beef variety meats to South Korea. The U.S. beef industry has lost up to $4 billion since the market closed, according to the U.S. Meat Export Federation.

The broader ban is expected to be lifted within days, pending publication of the government's new import regulations.

"We will be forced to make a critical decision if the government pushes through its plan to announce resumption of beef imports," said Sohn Hak-kyu, leader of the main opposition United Democratic Party, according to Yonhap. # South Korea to Lift Restrictions on Most American Beef Imports

SEOUL, South Korea (CNN) -- A high-ranking South Korean official disclosed on Thursday that the country plans to reopen its market to the majority of beef products from the United States, based on reporting from state-controlled media outlets. This announcement comes even as large crowds continue demonstrating in the streets of the capital against the agreement.

The origins of this dispute trace back to 2003, when South Korea imposed a complete halt on American beef imports following the discovery of a mad cow disease case within the U.S. This action eliminated what had previously been the third-most valuable overseas market for American beef producers. A partial reopening occurred the following year, permitting shipments of boneless meat sourced from cattle younger than 30 months—though this arrangement faced repeated disruptions before being fully terminated in October 2007.

According to Agriculture Minister Chung Woon-chun's statements to South Korea's Yonhap news agency on Thursday, the terms negotiated between the two nations last month prohibit importing particularly dangerous animal parts—including tonsils, brain tissue, spinal cord marrow, and portions of small intestine—as these components carry the highest likelihood of spreading mad cow disease to human consumers. Officials indicated the restrictions would be formally rescinded within a matter of days, pending publication of revised import regulations by the government.

This move toward resuming American beef shipments has proven politically costly for President Lee Myung-bak, who issued a public apology last week acknowledging he had underestimated public anxiety surrounding mad cow disease. Since news of the beef agreement broke, downtown Seoul has witnessed near-constant demonstrations, with participants regularly chanting slogans rejecting what they call "crazy cows."

The primary opposition faction has escalated its resistance to the deal. Sohn Hak-kyu, who heads the United Democratic Party, warned through Yonhap that "we will be forced to make a critical decision if the government pushes through its plan to announce resumption of beef imports," adding that failure to heed this caution would prompt his party to pursue "every possible measure to stop them." The opposition has already initiated legal action seeking to block enforcement of the new beef import provisions, Yonhap reported.

Meanwhile, President Lee's Grand National Party (GNP) has been working to defuse the controversy, insisting that American beef poses no health risk and that appropriate protective measures have been implemented. Party policy chief Lee Hahn-koo told Yonhap that "the government has tried its best to free the public from unnecessary concerns, and sufficient countermeasures have been prepared."

The April agreement reopening South Korea's beef market simultaneously cleared away a significant barrier that had been blocking U.S. congressional ratification of the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. President Lee has pressed the National Assembly to approve this trade pact without delay, arguing it would inject much-needed momentum into Korea's struggling economy by generating an estimated 300,000 jobs. However, opposition lawmakers have vowed to continue blocking the FTA unless the beef arrangement is scrapped entirely.

Prior to the 2003 ban, American exporters had shipped 815 million pounds worth of beef and related meat products to South Korean buyers. Industry estimates from the U.S. Meat Export Federation suggest American beef producers have sustained losses approaching $4 billion during the years the Korean market remained closed.

# South Korea to Lift U.S. Beef Import Ban Amid Public Outcry

South Korea is poised to lift its long-standing ban on most U.S. beef imports within days, according to a senior government official, pending the formal publication of new import regulations. The move marks the end of a five-year restriction that has strained trade relations between the two countries and represents a significant, if contentious, step in bilateral trade normalization.

## Background of the Ban

The original prohibition was enacted in 2003 following the discovery of a case of mad cow disease—formally known as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE)—in the United States. The discovery prompted immediate concern among South Korean regulators and consumers alike, leading to a comprehensive ban on American beef products. At the time, South Korea represented the third-largest export market for U.S. beef producers, making the closure a substantial blow to the American cattle industry and setting the stage for years of negotiations aimed at restoring market access.

## Terms of the New Agreement

Under the newly negotiated deal, South Korea will permit the resumption of most U.S. beef imports, but with specific safeguards in place. The agreement stipulates that high-risk materials—those tissues most closely associated with the transmission of mad cow disease—will remain prohibited. This includes tonsils, brain tissue, spinal cord marrow, and portions of the small intestine. By targeting these specific components, regulators aim to significantly reduce the risk of BSE transmission while still allowing the broader resumption of beef trade between the two nations.

## Political and Public Backlash

The announcement has ignited considerable political controversy and public unrest within South Korea. Thousands of protesters have taken to the streets of Seoul, voicing their opposition through demonstrations that included chants disparaging what demonstrators termed "crazy cows"—a pointed reference to mad cow disease and public fears over food safety. The scale and intensity of these protests have underscored deep-seated public anxiety about the safety of American beef, regardless of the new restrictions on high-risk materials.

The public pressure has reached the highest levels of government, with President Lee Myung-bak issuing a formal apology. In his statement, the president acknowledged that his administration had underestimated the depth of public concern surrounding the beef import issue, a rare admission that reflects the political sensitivity of the matter and the potential damage to his administration's credibility.

## Opposition Response

The controversy has also manifested in formal legal and political challenges. South Korea's main opposition party has filed a lawsuit seeking to suspend implementation of the new import terms, arguing that the government's approach fails to adequately protect public health and safety. Opposition leaders have gone further, explicitly threatening additional actions should the government proceed with its plan to lift the ban despite the legal challenge and ongoing public protests.

This combination of street demonstrations, presidential apology, and formal legal action illustrates the complex intersection of trade policy, public health concerns, and domestic politics that continues to complicate the resolution of this long-running trade dispute. As South Korea moves toward finalizing the new import rules, the government faces the challenge of balancing its trade commitments with the United States against significant domestic political pressure and public skepticism about food safety standards.

# South Korea's Vibrant Capital: A Look at Seoul

Seoul, the bustling capital of South Korea, stands as one of Asia's most dynamic and captivating cities. Home to nearly 10 million people, this sprawling metropolis seamlessly blends ancient traditions with cutting-edge modernity, creating a unique urban experience unlike any other in the world.

## A City of Contrasts

Walking through Seoul, visitors encounter a fascinating juxtaposition of old and new. Centuries-old palaces like Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung stand in the shadow of gleaming skyscrapers, while traditional hanok villages such as Bukchon offer glimpses into Korea's rich cultural heritage just minutes away from ultra-modern shopping districts like Gangnam and Myeongdong.

## Economic Powerhouse

As South Korea's political, economic, and cultural center, Seoul serves as the headquarters for major global corporations including Samsung, LG, and Hyundai. The city's economic influence extends far beyond its borders, contributing significantly to South Korea's position as one of Asia's most advanced economies.

## Cultural Influence

Seoul has become the epicenter of the "Korean Wave" (Hallyu), which has propelled K-pop, Korean dramas, and Korean cinema to global prominence. Districts like Hongdae pulse with youthful energy, live music venues, and street performances, while the entertainment industry continues to shape global pop culture trends.

## Culinary Delights

The city's food scene is equally impressive, offering everything from traditional Korean barbecue and kimchi jjigae to innovative fusion cuisine. Markets like Gwangjang Market provide authentic street food experiences, while Seoul's café culture rivals that of any major world city.

## Technology and Innovation

South Korea's reputation for technological advancement is evident throughout Seoul, from its efficient public transportation system to widespread high-speed internet connectivity. The city consistently ranks among the world's most technologically advanced urban centers.

Seoul truly represents the beating heart of South Korea—a city where tradition and innovation coexist, creating an ever-evolving urban landscape that continues to captivate visitors and residents alike.

# South Korea Lifts Ban on U.S. Beef Imports Despite Public Outcry

**SEOUL, South Korea** — The South Korean government announced Thursday it would lift restrictions on American beef imports, reopening a market that has been a persistent flashpoint in U.S.-Korea trade relations, even as demonstrators gathered outside government offices to protest the decision.

The move ends years of restrictions that were first imposed after cases of mad cow disease, or bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), were detected in American cattle. South Korea had banned or limited U.S. beef imports at various points, citing food safety concerns, despite reassurances from U.S. agricultural officials and international health bodies that American beef met global safety standards.

Agriculture Ministry officials said the decision followed extensive negotiations with Washington and was based on updated scientific risk assessments showing minimal danger to consumers.

"This decision was not made lightly," a ministry spokesperson said at a press briefing. "We have conducted thorough reviews of U.S. food safety protocols and believe the resumption of imports poses no significant risk to public health."

But the announcement was met with immediate backlash. Hundreds of protesters, many carrying signs reading "Health Before Trade" and "Our Food, Our Choice," gathered near the presidential office in central Seoul. Civic groups and farmers' associations, who fear cheaper American beef will undercut domestic producers, organized much of the demonstration.

"This is about more than beef," said Kim Min-jung, a protest organizer with a consumer advocacy coalition. "It's about whether our government listens to its own people or bows to outside pressure."

The beef issue has long carried outsized political weight in South Korea, dating back to massive candlelight protests in 2008 that drew hundreds of thousands into the streets and nearly derailed the government of then-President Lee Myung-bak. Critics say the latest decision risks reopening old wounds.

Farmers' groups also voiced economic concerns, warning that an influx of American beef could devastate local cattle industries already struggling with rising feed costs and shrinking profit margins.

"We cannot compete with subsidized American agriculture," said Park Jong-soo, head of a regional farmers' cooperative. "This will hurt Korean families who depend on this industry."

U.S. officials welcomed the announcement. A spokesperson for the U.S. Trade Representative's office called it "a positive step forward" in strengthening economic ties between the two allies and said American beef exporters have long sought greater access to the Korean market, one of the largest importers of beef in Asia.

Trade analysts say the decision may be linked to broader diplomatic and economic negotiations between Seoul and Washington, including discussions on tariffs, defense cost-sharing, and regional security cooperation amid tensions with North Korea.

South Korean President's office defended the move as necessary for maintaining strong bilateral relations, while pledging to increase inspections and labeling requirements to reassure consumers.

"We understand the public's concerns," a presidential spokesperson said. "That is why we are implementing strict monitoring systems to ensure the highest safety standards are met."

Despite these assurances, opposition lawmakers have called for parliamentary hearings on the decision, and some have threatened to introduce legislation to delay implementation.

As protests continued into the evening, it remained unclear whether public pressure might prompt the government to revisit elements of the policy. For now, officials say the new import rules will take effect within the coming weeks, marking a significant shift in a trade dispute that has simmered for more than a decade.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

# South Korea-US Beef Dispute of 2008: Background Report

## Overview

In the spring of 2008, South Korea witnessed massive public protests following the government's decision to resume imports of American beef, reigniting a controversy that had been dormant since 2003.

## Political Context

**Presidential Transition**
Lee Myung-bak had just assumed the presidency in February 2008, succeeding Roh Moo-hyun. Lee, a conservative former Hyundai executive and Seoul mayor, campaigned on pledges to revitalize the economy and strengthen the South Korea-US alliance, which had grown strained under his liberal predecessors.

**Timing and Diplomacy**
The beef import decision came just before Lee's first summit with President George W. Bush in April 2008. Critics argued the agreement was rushed to secure a successful summit and demonstrate goodwill toward Washington, raising concerns that food safety was sacrificed for diplomatic optics.

**Public Trust Deficit**
Many South Koreans felt the negotiations lacked transparency and public input. This fueled perceptions that Lee's government was prioritizing alliance management over domestic health concerns, contributing to a broader narrative of an administration disconnected from public sentiment.

## Economic Context

**Trade Relations Background**
The United States had banned South Korean beef imports intermittently and pushed for reopened access as part of broader trade normalization efforts, including negotiations around the Korea-US Free Trade Agreement (KORUS FTA), which was signed in 2007 but awaited ratification by both legislatures.

**Mad Cow Disease Concerns**
The core issue traced back to 2003, when the U.S. detected its first case of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE, or "mad cow disease"), prompting South Korea to ban American beef imports. The 2008 deal would lift restrictions on beef from cattle of all ages, a more lenient standard than many South Koreans expected or trusted, given international scientific debates over BSE risk by cattle age.

**Agricultural Industry Impact**
Domestic South Korean cattle farmers voiced strong opposition, fearing that resumed American imports—often cheaper—would undermine local beef producers already facing competitive pressures from anticipated FTA-related market openings.

## Resulting Unrest

The announcement triggered widespread candlelight vigils and protests across Seoul and other cities, drawing hundreds of thousands of participants at their peak. Demonstrators cited both public health fears and broader grievances about Lee's governance style. The protests marked one of the most significant early challenges to Lee's presidency and forced the government to renegotiate import terms with Washington to address safety concerns, including age restrictions on imported cattle.

---

*This dispute illustrates how trade policy, public health anxiety, and political trust can intersect to produce significant social mobilization, particularly during periods of leadership transition and shifting international alliances.*

# South Korea's Beef Ban Saga: From 2003 Restrictions to 2008 Protests

## The 2003 Ban

South Korea banned U.S. beef imports in December 2003 after the discovery of a case of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), commonly known as "mad cow disease," in a Holstein cow in Washington state. The animal had been imported from Canada, but its detection on U.S. soil prompted immediate action from South Korean health authorities, who suspended all imports of American beef as a precautionary measure.

The ban was part of a broader wave of restrictions imposed by dozens of countries worldwide following the U.S. case, reflecting global anxiety about BSE, which had devastated the British beef industry in the 1990s and been linked to variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, a fatal brain disorder in humans believed to result from consuming contaminated beef products.

Prior to the ban, the United States had been one of South Korea's largest beef suppliers, and the restriction dealt a significant blow to American cattle producers, who lobbied consistently for the resumption of exports to the lucrative Korean market.

## The 2008 Deal

In April 2008, South Korea and the United States reached an agreement to lift the beef ban, timed closely with a summit between then-President Lee Myung-bak and President George W. Bush. The deal was widely seen as a goodwill gesture ahead of broader negotiations on the Korea-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (KORUS FTA), which both governments were eager to advance.

Under the terms of the agreement, South Korea agreed to lift restrictions on U.S. beef imports, including allowing beef from cattle older than 30 months—a category previously considered higher risk for BSE transmission because the disease has a long incubation period and is more commonly detected in older animals. The deal also eased restrictions on certain cuts, including some previously banned parts such as brains, spinal cords, and other specified risk materials that scientists have identified as more likely to carry infectious prions if an animal is infected.

South Korean negotiators maintained that the deal included safeguards, such as provisions allowing Seoul to suspend imports again if new BSE cases emerged in the U.S., but critics argued the terms were far more lenient than restrictions maintained by other countries, including Japan, which continued to limit imports to beef from cattle 20 months or younger.

## Public Backlash

The agreement ignited an intense public backlash in South Korea, tapping into deep-seated anxieties about food safety and perceptions that the Lee government had prioritized diplomatic and trade relations with Washington over public health protections.

Beginning in May 2008, mass candlelight vigils erupted in Seoul and other cities, drawing tens of thousands of participants—by some estimates, crowds exceeded 100,000 people during peak demonstrations. What started as protests specifically about beef imports evolved into broader expressions of dissatisfaction with President Lee's administration, which had only taken office months earlier, in February 2008.

Protesters cited fears about human variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, distributed graphic images purporting to show its effects, and criticized what they viewed as an opaque negotiation process conducted without adequate parliamentary oversight or public consultation. Some demonstrations turned violent, with clashes between protesters and police resulting in arrests and injuries on both sides.

Facing sustained public pressure, the Lee government ultimately renegotiated aspects of the deal in June 2008, agreeing to voluntary restrictions ensuring that only beef from cattle younger than 30 months would be imported, effectively narrowing the terms of the original agreement without formally reopening treaty negotiations with Washington.

## Aftermath

The controversy significantly damaged President Lee's early approval ratings and prompted a cabinet reshuffle, as his administration sought to recover public trust. The episode became a notable case study in South Korean politics regarding the tension between trade liberalization commitments and domestic public health sentiment, and it complicated the broader ratification process for the KORUS FTA, which was not fully implemented until 2012, years after the initial framework had been negotiated.

The beef trade dispute remains a frequently cited example of how food safety concerns can become flashpoints for broader political discontent, particularly when intertwined with international trade negotiations and questions of national sovereignty over public health standards.
